question: How should a practitioner curate, synthesize, verify and process training data (mainly for post-training) so that a model gets data of enough quality, coverage and quantity?
contributions: Frames data curation by three criteria: quality, coverage, quantity.
Surveys data acquisition, augmentation, rule-based, simulation and AI-powered synthesis, with Llama 3 as a case study of instruction-data synthesis.
Covers verification of synthetic data, its limits, model distillation, and data processing (inspect, deduplicate, clean, format).

limits: Book chapter: most numbers are quoted from other work and the chapter gives no setup beyond a sentence for many of them (Databricks 20% and 60% has no model, dataset or metric).
Written in 2024: model and licence statements, and the claim that none of the model-collapse papers gives a safe synthetic-to-real ratio, may have dated.
Nemotron-4 and Li et al. synthetic-data successes were for one model iteration only, as the chapter says.
Chapter says it focuses on post-training data and brings in pre-training lessons only when insightful.
practices: Match data to the training phase: self-supervised sequences, (instruction, response), (instruction, winning, losing) or ((instruction, response), score) (Data Curation).
Judge data on quality, coverage and quantity; quality means relevant, aligned with task requirements, consistent, correctly formatted, sufficiently unique, compliant (Data Quality).
Choose a data mix that reflects real application usage, or run small-model scaling experiments per candidate mix (Data Coverage).
Start with a small well-made dataset (e.g. 50 examples) to see whether finetuning helps before curating a large one (Data Quantity).
Estimate extra data needs by finetuning on 25%, 50%, 100% subsets and plotting the curve (Data Quantity).
With little data use PEFT on more advanced models; with a lot, full finetuning on smaller models (Data Quantity).
Reduce high-quality data needs by staging: self-supervised then supervised, less-relevant then relevant, synthetic then real (Data Quantity tip).
Check dataset licences and provenance; never fully trust public data (Resources for publicly available datasets).
Write annotation guidelines; they are the same as evaluation guidelines (Data Acquisition and Annotation).
Use human-written responses with AI-generated instructions (reverse instruction) to avoid hallucinated long responses (Instruction data synthesis).

Verify synthetic data by execution, unit tests, back-translation, AI judges, classifiers, topic checks and heuristics; ask a judge twice with order swapped and keep triplets only if the winner agrees (AI-Powered Data Synthesis; Data verification).
Mix synthetic with human data rather than replacing it, and use only verified self-generated data when bootstrapping (Limitations; Model Distillation).
Check model licences before distilling, since many forbid training competing models (Model Distillation note).
Inspect data first: plot lengths and token distributions, compute inter-annotator disagreement, and manually look at examples (Inspect Data).

Deduplicate (pairwise, hashing such as MinHash or Bloom filter, dimensionality reduction), clean HTML/PII, then format to the model's chat template and keep prompts matching the finetuning format (Deduplicate; Clean and Filter; Format Data).
Keep a copy of original data, trial-run processing scripts, and order steps by cost (Data Processing tip).

tries to improve AI performance by enhancing the models themselves

generates data to mimic the properties of real data

the bot learned by playing against itself
a small model (student) is trained to mimic a larger model (teacher)
recursively using AI-generated data in training causes irreversible defects in the resulting models, degrading their performance over time
take existing long-form, high-quality content and use AI to generate prompts that would elicit such content
